title: Don't Give Away Your Best Weapon For Free
documentTitle: Email from Drew Bradstock to Jonathan Bellack et al. Re: Technorati Releases Tech To Manage Multiple Header Bidding Partners (July 21–22, 2015)
excerptForBlog:
We do not want to fully embrace header bidding as we are giving away a cheap form of dynamic allocation for free to all our competitors. This would have a large distorting effect on our rate card as one of the largest advantages to AdX is real time competition. In many regions, especially EMEA we have given away DFP at huge discounts to get access to inventory via DA.

Jonathan Bellack added: "We definitely should not be endorsing header bidding. We believe it is not good for users."

Assaf Grabinsky noted: "This will affect a small % of impressions that are the most valuable in the auction as those will get sold before EDA. In EMEA we are getting partner questions on this topic almost daily now... Given the surge in interest it seems we need a clear story for our sales teams: are we ignoring this for now due to ramping up of FLD and EDA in sponsorship, or rather should we go with a public stance embracing header bidders as rate setting signals for DFP that are fully compatible with Dynamic Allocation?"

lessonTitle: Don't Give Away Your Best Weapon For Free
pullQuote: When competitors find a cheap workaround to your premium product, the real question isn't whether to fight it — it's whether your pricing power survives if you don't.
leadershipTraits: slow to commit to a public stance
field teams push HQ for clarity
situation: In July 2015, Google's Drew Bradstock wrote internally to a group of colleagues about a competitor — Technorati — releasing technology that let publishers run multiple ad buyers simultaneously, a practice called header bidding. The core concern: if Google endorsed this approach, it would hand competitors the same real-time auction capability that made Google's AdX exchange uniquely valuable. Bradstock, Bellack, and Grabinsky are debating whether to embrace, ignore, or oppose the trend.
insight: Bradstock's line — 'we are giving away a cheap form of dynamic allocation for free to all our competitors' — names the real fear precisely. Google's 'dynamic allocation' let AdX compete for every impression in real time. That was a structural moat. Header bidding threatened to dissolve it by giving every rival the same last-look privilege. This is a classic competitive moat problem: the advantage isn't the technology itself, it's the exclusive access the technology enforces. Grabinsky sharpens the urgency — 'partner questions on this topic almost daily' in EMEA — and frames the internal fork clearly: do you stay silent, or do you get ahead of it with a public stance? The team never resolves that fork in this document, which tells you something about how hard the tradeoff actually was.
application: If a feature or integration you offer is what keeps customers from switching, map it explicitly before a competitor commoditizes it. Ask: if a free, open version of this existed, why would anyone still pay for mine? Build your next defensible layer before that question answers itself in the market.
